title: The Other Captivity: When the Faith Dissolves Into a Cause
subtitle: The right makes Christianity the conservative platform at prayer. The left makes it the progressive platform at prayer. By opposite doors, both hand over the same thing.

sections.title: The Captivity We Do Not Name
sections.body:
This platform has spent most of its breath on one captivity. The cross wrapped in a flag. The gospel enlisted as the chaplain of a political party. The church that mistook access to power for faithfulness. That critique was earned, and I stand by every word of it. But a guardrail that only ever fires in one direction has stopped being a conviction and become a team jersey. There is another way out of the faith, older and quieter than Christian nationalism, and it does not open to the right. It opens to the left, and it is the one my own instincts are more likely to walk through.

The temptation on the right is to make Christianity a weapon. The temptation on the left is subtler and, for a certain kind of thoughtful believer, more seductive. It is to make the faith so reasonable, so kind, so aligned with the conscience of the educated and the decent, that it no longer asks anyone to believe anything a modern person would find embarrassing. No blood. No wrath. No empty tomb that a coroner would have to explain. Just love, justice, and a Jesus who happens to agree with us about everything.

I want to give that impulse its due before I name what it costs, because at its root it is not a betrayal of the gospel. It is the gospel remembering something the other side forgot. And then, one quiet subtraction at a time, it becomes a different thing entirely. This is not a story about villains. It is a story about good people who loved their neighbors and slowly misplaced their Lord.

sections.title: Rauschenbusch and the Good That Was Real
sections.body:
Walter Rauschenbusch was a Baptist pastor before he was a symbol, and he earned his convictions in Hell's Kitchen. In the 1880s and 1890s he buried the children of German immigrants who were ground down by an economy that treated them as fuel. He watched the revivalists preach a gospel that saved souls and said nothing to the sweatshop, and he decided that a faith that small was not the faith of the prophets. In Christianity and the Social Crisis in 1907, and A Theology for the Social Gospel in 1917, he built the case that sin is not only a stain on the individual heart but a poison in the structures that individuals build together.

He was not making it up. He was reading his Bible. Amos thundered that God despised the solemn assemblies and wanted instead that justice roll down like waters, and righteousness like an ever-flowing stream. Jesus opened his ministry in Nazareth by claiming the words of Isaiah, good news to the poor, liberty to the captives. In Matthew 25 he said the nations would be sorted by how they treated the least of these. The Social Gospel saw a body attached to the soul, and it was right to see it.

Martin Luther King Jr. would later credit Rauschenbusch with giving him a theological grounding for social concern, even while warning that Rauschenbusch came close to identifying the Kingdom of God with a particular social order. Hold both halves. The impulse to defend the vulnerable and confront structural evil is not the enemy of the gospel. It is the gospel refusing to be only private. Whatever went wrong later did not go wrong here.

sections.title: The Subtraction
sections.body:
Watch what happened underneath the good. To make the faith speak fluently to the social crisis, its hardest edges were quietly filed off, not by argument but by embarrassment. The miracles began to feel like a liability in a scientific age. The resurrection became a beautiful symbol of renewal and hope, no longer a corpse that walked out of a tomb on the third day. Sin was relocated entirely into systems and structures, where it indicted everyone in general and no one in the mirror. And the atonement, the blood, the wrath of God satisfied at the cross, came to seem primitive, even barbaric, something an enlightened faith should apologize for and move past.

Name the mechanism precisely, because it never announces itself. This is not denial by frontal assault. Nobody stood up and voted to cancel the empty tomb. It is subtraction by embarrassment. One doctrine at a time, quietly set down because it did not play well in the room the church wanted to be respected in. The offense was not refuted. It was retired.

H. Richard Niebuhr wrote the epitaph in 1937, describing where the liberal Protestantism of his day had arrived. It preached, he said, a God without wrath who brought men without sin into a kingdom without judgment through the ministrations of a Christ without a cross. Read that slowly and count what is gone. Wrath, sin, judgment, cross. What remains is a warm ethical glow with the name of Jesus attached, and a warm ethical glow cannot raise the dead. It can only agree with the living.

sections.title: Machen Saw It First
sections.body:
The fight came to a head in the 1920s, in the controversy that split the northern Presbyterians and Baptists down the middle. In 1922, from the pulpit of First Presbyterian Church in New York, the modernist preacher Harry Emerson Fosdick asked whether the fundamentalists would win, and the battle was joined in public. The best mind on the other side belonged to J. Gresham Machen, a New Testament scholar at Princeton Seminary, and in 1923 he wrote the book that still frames the question. It is called Christianity and Liberalism, and its argument is merciless in its clarity.

Machen did not say the liberals were bad Christians. He said something far more unsettling. He argued that liberalism was not a variety of the Christian religion at all, but a different religion entirely, one that had borrowed Christian words and drained them of their original meaning. He was courteous toward liberals as people and unbending on the substance. The question, he insisted, was not conservative temperament against progressive temperament. It was whether the faith rests on events that actually happened, a real incarnation, a real cross, a real bodily resurrection, or whether it rests on values that those old stories merely illustrate and could survive without.

Subtract the events and keep the values, Machen said, and you have not produced a modernized Christianity. You have produced a new religion wearing the old vocabulary like borrowed clothes. It was a hard verdict, and much of the church dismissed it as reactionary. Then the century ran the experiment for him. On the one point that finally mattered, the scholar from Princeton turned out to be a prophet.

sections.title: The Mainline Emptied
sections.body:
The experiment has results, and they are not seriously in dispute. The mainline Protestant denominations, the Methodists and Presbyterians and Episcopalians and Congregationalists, were once the established center of American life, the churches of presidents and universities and the cultural establishment. Since their peak in the mid-1960s they have lost members by the millions, decade after decade, shrinking from the mainstream to a remnant while the country around them grew. Ross Douthat told the story in Bad Religion in 2012, tracing how the accommodating churches hollowed out even as they congratulated themselves on their relevance.

Be fair about the causes, because they are contested. Birthrates, education, mobility, and the general secularizing drift all did real work, and no honest account blames theology alone. But the theological point survives every qualification. A church that has subtracted the offense until nothing it teaches would surprise a decent secular liberal has given no one a reason to walk through its doors, and fewer reasons to stay. Gary Dorrien, the liberal tradition's own most careful and sympathetic historian, chronicles its genuine brilliance across three volumes, and also its long dissolution.

Here is the verdict the numbers keep pointing at. A Christianity that agrees with the age can comfort the age, but it cannot convert it, because it has nothing to say that the age was not already telling itself. The cross was never good marketing. It was the whole message. Remove it to win the room, and you keep the room and lose the only reason you were ever standing in it.

sections.title: The Same Trade By Opposite Doors
sections.body:
So set the two captivities side by side, because they are more alike than either would ever admit. The church of the right keeps the supernatural and loses the ethics. It confesses the empty tomb on Sunday and baptizes power on Monday, conscripting the cross into a flag and calling the exchange courage. The church of the left keeps the ethics and loses the supernatural. It marches for the poor and quietly buries the resurrection, baptizing the conscience of the age and calling the exchange maturity. Different doors. Same trade. Each hands over the half of the faith its own tribe finds embarrassing, and each is left holding a Christianity that is a mirror of what it already believed before it walked in.

I have felt both pulls, and the left one pulls harder on a man like me, who would rather be thought thoughtful than be thought naive. That is exactly why I have to name it. The forbidden thing, the offense that neither tribe can sell, is the one thing either tribe was ever given to preach. A crucified God is an embarrassment to the powerful and an embarrassment to the enlightened, and it was always supposed to be. That embarrassment is the gospel.

So the question that remains is not which captivity is worse. It is whether there is a church left that will keep the whole thing, the cross and the justice, the wrath and the mercy, the empty tomb and the least of these, when keeping all of it costs the applause of both rooms. That church will not be comfortable in either tribe. It was never meant to be.
